query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: For multi‐element near‐equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, reducing the noble metal fraction enhances high-temperature structural and chemical stability by increasing overall mixing entropy and suppressing the driving forces for phase segregation and intermetallic formation.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles synthesized as multi-element, near-equiatomic solid solutions (including a mixture of noble and non-noble/refractory elements) via physical/chemical fabrication methods.
generation.intervention: Systematically reduce the noble metal content during synthesis and compare these formulations with higher noble metal content controls, while monitoring structural and compositional evolution under high-temperature catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) service-simulated conditions.
generation.conditions: Exposure to controlled high-temperature regimes representative of catalytic and thermoelectric service environments, using atmospheres and durations that replicate realistic operational conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The atomic-scale mixing state and high configurational entropy in the nanoparticle solid solution, which mitigate phase separation and intermetallic formation.
generation.mechanism: Lowering the noble metal content reduces segregation tendencies that can otherwise promote the formation of distinct phases or intermetallic compounds at elevated temperatures. The increased proportion of refractory/base metals preserves the random solid-solution structure by maintaining high mixing entropy, thereby preventing chemical degradation and structural transformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under service-regime conditions, nanoparticles with reduced noble metal content will display less evidence of phase separation (as measured by in situ XRD and TEM), retain a more homogeneous elemental distribution (verified by XPS/EDS), and show improved stability relative to the baseline high noble metal content nanoparticles.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles with standard or higher noble metal fractions synthesized under otherwise similar conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for nanoparticles with near-equiatomic solid-solution compositions; however, if the noble metal content is reduced excessively, it may negatively impact the catalytic function despite enhanced stability. The hypothesis is most applicable in systems where the noble metal plays a secondary structural role.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal noble metal reduction threshold that balances catalytic activity with structural stability has yet to be precisely determined, and interactions with other compositional variables may modulate the effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of near-equiatomic nanoparticles: one with a standard (higher) noble metal fraction and one with a significantly reduced noble metal fraction. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature testing conditions that simulate catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) environments. Use operando XRD to monitor phase evolution and TEM/XPS to assess chemical homogeneity over time.
measurements: Phase purity and any evolution of secondary phases via XRD
Microstructural changes and particle morphology by TEM
Elemental distribution and oxidation state by XPS/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with reduced noble metal content do not display a statistically significant improvement in retaining a single-phase, homogeneous solid-solution structure (i.e., if similar levels of phase separation, chemical degradation, or intermetallic formation are observed in both sets) then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ]. Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

chosen.technique: systematic synthesis coupled with operando high-temperature structural and chemical characterization (XRD, XPS, TEM)
chosen.conditions: durations at catalytic temperatures (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric temperatures (473–1923 K) that replicate service environments, emphasizing formulations with reduced noble-metal loadings
chosen.why: This move directly addresses the performance limitation niche by intervening on the nanoparticle composition – specifically the noble metal fraction – to decouple its influence on stability. It leverages standard high-temperature synthesis and operando characterization methods common in the field, thereby providing a clear mechanistic test of whether reduced noble-metal content can preserve structural and chemical stability under realistic service conditions, and thus offers a decisive falsification test of competing stabilization mechanisms.
